notes:
I've put together notes for every verse. Some limits first:

- **Tool limits.** I ran out of tool calls before I could read sources from desiringgod, gty, TGC, Ligonier, Lutheran sites, oca.org, catholic.com or bibleodyssey. Nothing from those sites appears here.
- **Partly read pages.** Augustine's sermon on newadvent cut off at section 7, so I only have his notes on vv. 1–4. I couldn't open Spurgeon's full page, so his v. 9 note and the Ellicott, Calvin and Ryle notes on vv. 2–4 are missing.
- **Traditions.** I found no real fight between denominations over this psalm. What I did find is individual teachers from different traditions disagreeing on particular points. I've labelled the tradition where the source names it.
- **Popular modern teaching.** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm. Verse 7 (trusting in riches) is the obvious place such a discussion would happen, but nothing turned up.
- **Untagged notes.** Points from Enduring Word, Augustine and the NET page I read in full are given with their URLs but without citation tags.

---

**Title (Doeg the Edomite)**
- **Traditional reading:** The background is 1 Samuel 21–22. Doeg told Saul that the priests at the tabernacle had helped David. Saul then had Doeg kill the priests. Guzik notes the psalm is a "Contemplation" that looks at the root and the end of Doeg's evil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
- Clarke adds that on his way to Achish, king of Gath, David passed through Nob, where the tabernacle then was. He took Goliath's sword there and, being very hungry, ate some of the shewbread. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-52.html
- **Another reading:** The Critical and Explanatory commentary reads part of the psalm as aimed at Saul. It says Saul was the one who "trusted in the abundance of his riches" (v. 7) as a means against David, and that the label "the Edomite" points to Edom as the representative of the world's hostility to God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-52.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** His manuscripts read "Abimelech" rather than "Ahimelech." He takes the change of name as a sign to look for a hidden spiritual meaning rather than only the history. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801052.htm

**v. 1**
- **"Mighty man" said with irony:** Guzik quotes Poole and Spurgeon. Killing 85 unarmed priests was hardly the act of a true warrior. Morgan notes that Coverdale translated the phrase "Thou Tyrant." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
- Ellicott (Anglican): "hero," used sarcastically. https://biblehub.com/psalms/52-1.htm
- **"The goodness of God endures":** Barnes says the wicked man could not hope to prevent the exercise of the divine goodness toward him whom he persecuted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-1.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist): the tyrant's fury cannot dry up God's mercy; if the priests are slain, their Master still lives, and he will outlive Doeg and put right his wrongs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-1.htm
- Gill (Baptist) sees God's goodness as what the saints boast in, set against Doeg's boasting. He also says the character well agrees with the little horn and Romish beast, Daniel 7:20. That anti-papal application is Gill's own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-1.htm
- Guzik notes that the word for God here is *El*, which some think stresses God's strength over against Doeg the "hero." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** The NET translates "God's loyal love protects me all day long." The Hebrew is literally "the loyal love of God [is] all the day." The note says the context, where the psalmist is under threat, suggests he is protected by God's loyal love at all times. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=Psa+52%3A1-5
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Strength is meant to be used for good. Destroying is easy: anyone can burn a crop or kill a child. A killer's "might" is no greater than a scorpion's or a poisonous mushroom's. "He that glories, let him glory in the Lord." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801052.htm

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the tongue revealed an evil heart. Maclaren notes the psalm stresses sins of speech because it traces the violent deeds back to their source. Poole compares the tongue to a razor that seems to shave but cuts the throat. Morgan points to what James says about the tongue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
- **NET:** "Your tongue carries out your destructive plans; it is as effective as a sharp razor, O deceiver." https://biblehub.com/net/psalms/52.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** "All day long" means the wicked man plots evil without stopping. Augustine treats the psalm as prophecy of what will happen to the wicked, not as a curse. The razor can only shave off "hair," meaning surplus earthly things. It cannot take what is eternal from saints who look to the kingdom of heaven. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801052.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Doeg loved both evil and lies. Quoting Boice, he says Doeg kept his information until it would serve him best. David took his share of blame for his own lie to Ahimelech (1 Sam 22:22) but rightly did not blame himself for the massacre. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Good and evil were both in front of Doeg, and he chose evil. The wicked condemn themselves, because they protest loudly when they are wronged. Loving malice above kindness is like trying to keep water on top of oil: in the end, malice sinks. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801052.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Doeg trusted in riches, likely gained by currying favor with King Saul through betrayal, and he loved the harm his "devouring words" did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/

**v. 5**
- **Four pictures of judgment:** A house torn down, a coal snatched from the fire, a person dragged from their tent, a tree pulled up by the roots. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
- Barnes: the verb translated "take away" is elsewhere used only in the sense of taking up and carrying fire or coals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-5.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican): this is the exact opposite of "pluck a brand from the burning"; the picture is of pulling the house-fire apart and so putting out family life. https://biblehub.com/psalms/52-5.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: God will destroy Doeg root and branch, as thou didst destroy the entire house of Ahimelech. https://biblehub.com/psalms/52-5.htm
- **Debate 1: prophecy or prayer?** Guzik quotes VanGemeren, who prefers to read the verbs as wishes ("may God bring you down…"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/ The Cambridge Bible grants the verbs could be read as a prayer, as in the Septuagint ("May God destroy thee"), but prefers the future: the sentence is pronounced with a prophet's authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-5.htm
- Augustine (Catholic) also reads the psalm as prophecy, not ill-will. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801052.htm
- **Debate 2: whose "tent"?** Barnes takes it as Doeg's own home. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-5.html
  - Matthew Henry reads it as not thy dwelling-place, but God's: Doeg will be cut off from God's favour and worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-5.html
  - Poole sees it as a kind of excommunication. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-5.htm
  - The Calvin edition's footnotes cite Hammond: the Septuagint reads "from the tabernacle," and the Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) speaks of the place of God's presence. They also cite Archbishop Secker, who contrasts this with David staying in God's house in v. 8. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_2/psalm_52_5-7.htm
- **Debate 3: how far does "forever" reach?** Gill (Baptist) takes it as body and soul in hell, with an everlasting destruction. He applies it to the antichristian party as well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-5.htm
  - Poole limits "land of the living" to out of this world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-5.htm
- **Reformed (Calvin):** David piles up the verbs rather for his own conviction and comfort, than with a view to alarming the conscience of the offender. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-5.html
- **NET:** "God will make you a permanent heap of ruins" (Hebrew: "will tear you down forever"). The rare verb for "scoop up" appears elsewhere only in Prov 6:27, 25:22 and Isa 30:14. http://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psalm 52:5-9

**v. 6**
- **"See and fear":** Pulpit Commentary: Every manifestation of the Divine power and justice produces in the righteous man a feeling of awe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-52.html
- **Debate: is the laughter right for believers?**
  - Pulpit Commentary: the laughter is something like derision of his fallen enemy—or, at least, it did not under the old covenant, when men had not yet been taught that they ought to "love" their enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-52.html
  - Calvin (Reformed): believers laugh not in the way of insulting over them, but rejoicing more and more in the confidence of the help of God. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_2/psalm_52_5-7.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch: it is joy that justice has finally broken through. Even the Old Testament (Proverbs 24:17) reprobates the low malignant joy that glories at the overthrow of one's enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-7.htm
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) quotes the view that the words show delight in God's moral government of the world, rather than personal vindictiveness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-52.html
  - Guzik quotes Maclaren, who defends the joy of oppressed people when tyrants fall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading:** Pulpit Commentary: The root of Doeg's wickedness was want of trust in God, and consequent alienation from him. To obtain wealth he became Saul's unscrupulous tool. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-52.html
- Calvin (Reformed): none can be said sincerely to repose upon God but he who has been emptied of all confidence in his own resources. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-7.html
- Matthew Henry: Doeg did not think that the continuance of his prosperity depended upon the favour of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-7.html
- **Spurgeon's gospel application (Baptist):** In his Treasury's "explanatory notes" section, under Spurgeon's name: While others trust in the riches of their own righteousness and services… do thou renounce all, and trust in the mercy of God in Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps052.cfm
- **Translation debate on the last line:** Calvin thinks the word usually rendered "wickedness" here means "substance." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-7.html
  - The Cambridge Bible says it may mean greed. The Aramaic and Syriac "in his wealth" seems to represent a slightly different reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-7.htm
  - NET translates "was confident about his plans to destroy others." It says "destruction" points back to v. 2, and it suggests a small correction to the Hebrew verb form. http://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psalm 52:5-9

**v. 8**
- **Contrast with v. 5:** The uprooted tree in v. 5 is set against the flourishing olive. Calvin (Reformed) says that though David looked more like a rotting trunk at the time, he compares himself, in the confidence of coming prosperity, to a green olive. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol09/htm/xviii.iii.htm
- **"Green" means vigorous:** Calvin's footnote says the Hebrew has no reference to the color of the tree, but to its fresh, vigouous and flourish condition. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_2/psalm_52_8-9.htm Ellicott agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-8.html
- **Debate: were there real trees at the sanctuary?**
  - Constable: The tree David saw was in the tabernacle courtyard, symbolic of his nearness to God.
  - Barnes: such a tree could have grown in the courts around the tabernacle.
  - Pulpit Commentary: it certainly cannot be proved that they were not.
  - Clarke: It does not mean that there were olive-trees planted in God's house; the picture is of David in God's house as an olive is in good soil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-52.html
  - Sources for the first three: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-8.html
- **What is "the house of God"?** Wesley (Methodist): In God's church, or among his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-8.html
  - The Cambridge Bible suggests it may also mean the land of Israel (Hosea 9:15), in which the righteous dwells securely while the wicked man is driven out of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-8.htm
- **"Mercy," not merit:** Matthew Henry: not in my own merit, but in God's mercy, which dispenses its gifts freely, even to the unworthy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/52-7.html
- **Wesleyan (Benson):** The olive renews itself with new shoots. David uses it to denote the stability and perpetuity of his prosperity, and that of his family. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-8.htm
- **NET:** The wording sharply contrasts the wicked man's fate (vv. 5–7) with the psalmist's security. "Forever and ever" may be poetic exaggeration for "continually." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Psa&chapter=52&tab=commentaries&verse=8

**v. 9**
- **"Because You have done it":** Guzik: David praises God in faith before Doeg's evil has been dealt with. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
  - NET translates "when you execute judgment." It takes the Hebrew perfect ("you have acted") as probably looking ahead to a vindication still to come: David will give thanks when it happens. http://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psalm 52:5-9
- Calvin (Reformed): David says it was entirely owing to the divine protection that he had escaped from the treachery of Doeg. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_2/psalm_52_8-9.htm
- Constable: David knew that what set him apart from Doeg was due to God's grace, not his own works. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-52.html
- **"Wait on Your name":** Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: let the mighty boast; we will wait on the Lord, and patience will have its reward. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-52/
  - NET: God's "name" means his reputation and revealed character. Literally, "it is good in front of your loyal followers." http://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psalm 52:5-9
  - Matthew Henry: nothing calms a troubled spirit or keeps us from crooked courses for our relief like quietly waiting for the Lord's salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/52-8.htm
- **"Your saints":** Calvin calls them God's "meek ones," because they reflect in their character the kindness and beneficence of their Father in heaven. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_2/psalm_52_8-9.htm
